question.prompt: Jacob uses the following procedure to write down a sequence of numbers. First he chooses the first term to be \(6.\) To generate each succeeding term, he flips a fair coin. If it comes up heads, he doubles the previous term and subtracts \(1.\) If it comes up tails, he takes half of the previous term and subtracts \(1.\) What is the probability that the fourth term in Jacob’s sequence is an integer?

solutions.explanation:
Reaching the fourth term requires three coin flips. The \(2^3=8\) possible head-tail histories are equally likely. Let \(H\) denote doubling and subtracting \(1\), and let \(T\) denote halving and subtracting \(1\). Following each history gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
HHH &: 6\to11\to21\to41,\\
HHT &: 6\to11\to21\to\frac{19}{2},\\
HTH &: 6\to11\to\frac92\to8,\\
HTT &: 6\to11\to\frac92\to\frac54,\\
THH &: 6\to2\to3\to5,\\
THT &: 6\to2\to3\to\frac12,\\
TTH &: 6\to2\to0\to-1,\\
TTT &: 6\to2\to0\to-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each three-flip history appears exactly once. The integer fourth terms occur for \(HHH,HTH,THH,TTH,TTT\). Although the last two histories end at the same number, they are distinct coin outcomes and both count. Thus the probability is \(\boxed{\frac58}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
solutions.title: Follow all eight coin-flip histories
